title: Reducing the Entanglement Cost of Distributed Bipartite Quantum Computation with Constant Qubit Overhead
authors: Kosuke Matsui, Jun-Yi Wu, Min-Hsiu Hsieh, Mio Murao
abstract: Distributed quantum computation connects multiple quantum processing units (QPUs) through quantum communication to jointly perform large-scale quantum computations. Since the number of qubits available at each QPU is limited, it is important to reduce quantum communication while keeping the qubit overhead small. To this end, we study an entanglement-assisted model, in which entanglement consumption serves as a measure of quantum communication cost. For exact deterministic implementations in this model, the operator Schmidt rank of the target bipartite unitary provides a general lower bound on entanglement cost when qubit overhead is unrestricted. However, it has remained unclear how closely this bound can be approached with constant qubit overhead. In this work, we show that this lower bound is attainable for every bipartite Clifford unitary using at most two auxiliary qubits per QPU. In addition, for non-Clifford unitaries specified by exact Clifford+$T$ decompositions with $T$-count $t$, we construct implementations with the same qubit overhead whose entanglement cost is at most $2t$ Bell pairs above this lower bound.
summary: This paper tackles the resource optimization challenge in distributed quantum computing by minimizing entanglement consumption. It shows that for Clifford unitaries, the minimum entanglement cost is achievable while keeping the required auxiliary qubits constant. For more complex unitaries, it provides a tight upper bound on the excess entanglement cost relative to the theoretical minimum.
main_problem: The paper addresses how to minimize the entanglement cost required for distributed bipartite quantum computation while strictly limiting the number of auxiliary qubits available at each processing unit.
main_result: They prove that the theoretical lower bound on entanglement cost is attainable for all bipartite Clifford unitaries using only two auxiliary qubits per QPU, and provide a tight bound for non-Clifford unitaries.
method: The authors utilize the operator Schmidt rank ($	ext{OpSch}$) as a lower bound and construct explicit quantum circuit implementations based on decomposing the target unitary into elementary blocks.
model_or_system: The model is distributed quantum computation connecting multiple Quantum Processing Units (QPUs) via quantum communication, analyzed in an entanglement-assisted setting using shared Bell pairs.
key_observables: Entanglement Cost (measured in Bell pairs), Qubit Overhead (number of auxiliary qubits required), and the Operator Schmidt Rank ($	ext{OpSch}(U)$).
important_parameters: The T-count ($t$) for non-Clifford unitaries, and the constant overhead limit (e.g., $\le (2, 2)$ qubits).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes perfect Bell pairs and focuses on exact deterministic implementations of the quantum gates.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the implementation of Clifford unitaries using specific Bell pairs and qubit overheads, showing decompositions into elementary blocks.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the general lower bound using $	ext{OpSch}(U)$, then proves attainability for Clifford unitaries with constant overhead, and finally derives an upper bound for non-Clifford unitaries based on their T-count.
why_interesting: This work provides concrete, resource-efficient protocols for large-scale quantum computation, directly impacting the feasibility of networking quantum processors.

FIG. 4. Distributed implementation of SWAP using two Bell pairs with qubit overhead (1, 2). The left and right dashed boxes show teleportation from Alice to Bob and from Bob to Alice, respectively. Each two-input measurement symbol abbreviates a Bell-basis measurement: a local CNOT gate and a Hadamard gate followed by two computational-basis measurements. Double lines carry the measurement outcomes to the squares representing Pauli corrections. Between the teleportations, Bob locally swaps the received state with his original input state, so the latter is teleported to Alice. Red braces indicate the qubit overhead.
